previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: The patient, a male with a history of Crohn’s disease status post subtotal colectomy, was admitted with fever and abdominal pain 36 hours after a social outing. He had recently been discharged from a prior admission with increased immunosuppression. Evaluation revealed an acute flare of Crohn’s disease confirmed by flexible sigmoidoscopy and biopsy, showing ulceration and inflammation at the ileosigmoid anastomosis. His elevated creatinine of 1.6 improved to 1.2 with IV hydration, resolving acute kidney injury. An 8mm nonobstructing kidney stone was found on renal ultrasound, contributing to his pain. He was treated with IV steroids, transitioned to oral prednisone, and given a course of ciprofloxacin due to fever in the setting of immunosuppression. The pain service initiated a PCA and started Flexeril, later transitioning to a short outpatient opioid supply. He tolerated a regular diet, and his symptoms improved. He was discharged home with follow-up arranged and instructions to monitor for worsening symptoms.

Brief Hospital Course:
___ man with history of ___ admitted with abdominal pain, 
diarrhea and acute renal failure.

1. Acute Flare of ___ Disease: 
Etiology of his acute worsening of abdominal pain and diarrhea 
was unclear. His symptoms were most likely related to an acute 
flare of his ___ Disease. CT Abd/Pelvis was relatively 
unremarkable. His imuran was held during this admission, and he 
was started on methylprednisolone 20mg IV q8h with IV pain 
medications and antiemetics. He briefly required a morphine PCA 
for pain control. He was initially NPO. As his abdominal pain 
slowly improved, his diet was advanced and he was transitioned 
to oral pain medications. Upon discharge, he was tolerating a 
full diet and taking pills. The gastroenterology consult team 
was involved with the patient's care during this admission. 

2. Hypercalcemia: 
Patient's calcium was elevated to 10.7 on admission. Etiology of 
this hypercalcemia was unclear, although his calcium levels were 
within normal range for the rest of his hospitalization. PTH was 
checked and was found to be slightly low at 14. Vitamin D levels 
were checked and were noted to be low. A letter was sent to the 
patient, his PCP, and his primary gastroenterologist with this 
information.  

3. Acute renal failure: 
Etiology was thought likely related to pre-renal etiology in the 
setting of dehydration and diarrhea. He was aggressively 
rehydrated, and his creatinine improved to baseline within 48 
hours of admission. 

4. GERD: 
He was maintained on PPI during this admission, initially IV and 
then transitioned to oral once tolerating regular diet. 

5. Anxiety: 
Upon admission, patient had not received his seroquel because 
his prescription ran out. His anxiety was under poor control on 
admission, and his symptoms improved with restarting his 
seroquel.

radiology_notes.text:
HISTORY:  ___ man, with Crohn's.  Now creatinine of 1.8. Assess for
Crohn's complications.

COMPARISON:  ___.

TECHNIQUE:  Non-IV contrast, MDCT images were acquired from the lung bases to
the pubic symphysis after administration of oral contrast.  Multiplanar
reformatted images were obtained for evaluation.

FINDINGS:

CT ABDOMEN WITHOUT IV CONTRAST, WITH P.O. CONTRAST:  The lung bases are clear.
The non-IV contrast study limits full evaluation of the intra-abdominal
parenchymal organs.  Allowing for the limitations, the liver is grossly normal
without focal lesions.  The gallbladder, pancreas, spleen, adrenal glands, and
kidneys are grossly normal.  There is no renal stone, hydronephrosis, or
hydroureter.  The stomach is moderately distended with food particle.  The
duodenum is normal in caliber.  There is good contrast passage from the
stomach through the duodenum to the distal small bowel.  No free air, fluid,
or lymphadenopathy is noted.

CT PELVIS WITHOUT IV CONTRAST, WITH P.O. CONTRAST:  The patient is status post
ileosigmoid anastomosis.  There is oral contrast passing through to the distal
ileum without evidence of small-bowel obstruction.  The wall of sigmoid colon
is within normal limits.  Normal fecal matter is noted in the sigmoid and
rectum.  The bladder is only mildly distended, but without focal abnormality. 
There is no free air, fluid or lymphadenopathy in the pelvis.

BONE WINDOW:  No suspicious lytic or sclerotic lesions are noted.

IMPRESSION:  No bowel obstruction.  Good passage of oral contrast through and
up to the distal ileum.  No free air, fluid or abscess.
